claim: Flowchart lexer cannot read a circle- or cross-ended link that has text between its dashes

triage.scenario: `A o-- text --o B` (or `x-- text --x`). The LINK match gives lead `o`, body `--` and no tail. The guard `(lead === 'o' || lead === 'x') && tail !== lead` returns false before the text-link path (`opens`/`linkText`) is tried. `o` is then lexed as a word, and the parser throws "expected the end of the statement, found "o"". The same link with `|text|` reads, so a valid Mermaid link form is refused. For an opening link, the guard should compare the lead with the closer's head that `linkText` returns.
triage.cause: lead/tail check runs before the text-link closer is known

claim: Flowchart lexer refuses link text that runs right up to its closing arrow
Flowchart, block and architecture writers rename ids their own readers accept (node-1, 1, a.b)

triage.scenario: The flowchart lexer's and block parser's `WORD` (`[\p{L}\p{N}_](?:[\p{L}\p{N}_]|[-.](?=…))*`) and architecture's `ID` (`[\p{L}\p{N}_][\p{L}\p{N}_-]*`) read `node-1`, `1` and `a.b` as ids. All three writers call `mermaidIds(…, { unicode: true })`, which only keeps ids matching `^[\p{L}_][\p{L}\p{N}_]*$`. So reading `flowchart TD\n 1 --> node-1` and writing it back gives `n1 --> node_1`: every id with a hyphen, a dot or a leading digit is renamed on a plain round trip. In the block writer, the reader's own minted anonymous group id `block-1` can never be written as itself either: once a span or an edge forces it to be named, it comes back as `block_1`. The writers should pass an `id` regex matching what their reader takes, as the class and ER writers already do.
triage.cause: writer's id grammar narrower than reader's

claim: Class diagram note text loses an `&` that comes right before a backslash

triage.scenario: a `note` shape whose text is `R&\D`. `spelled()` runs `spelledBreaks` first, and it leaves the `&` alone because nothing after it looks like an entity yet. Only after that does `.replace(/\\/g, '#92;')` turn the backslash into `#92;`, so the line written is `note "R\D"`. On read, `decodeEntities(l, true)` matches `\` as one HTML numeric reference, and the note comes back as `R\D`. The `&` is silently lost. It should come back as `R&\D`: the `&` needs to be spelled `#38;` once the `#92;` exists, which means escaping `\` before `spelledBreaks` runs.
triage.cause: an entity is added after the `&` guard has already run

claim: Flowchart writer silently writes a path outline node as a rectangle, with no warning

triage.scenario: a node whose `outline` is a `Path` (the `Outline` type is `BuiltinOutline | string | Path`) is written. `brackets` is undefined, but the warning only fires when `typeof outline === 'string'`, so the node comes out as `id["…"]` (a rectangle) with no warning. It should warn as it does for an unknown string outline. The block writer (`block/write.ts` `block()`) warns whenever `brackets === undefined`, so the two writers handle the same case differently.
triage.cause: warning gated on a string outline

claim: ER writer lets an entity id be `accTitle`/`accDescr`; an entity with attributes then reads as accessibility text or throws
The gantt, gitGraph and journey writers drop a page name that differs from the chart title, without the warning the other chart kinds give
Gantt writer emits a bare `section` or `title` line for an empty name

triage.scenario: a gantt whose section `name` is `''` (the local reader produces this from a bare `section` line), or whose `title` is `''` or only whitespace. The writer tests only `!== undefined`, so it writes `  section ` / `  title `. Mermaid's gantt grammar needs text after either keyword, so its parser rejects the file. An empty name should be treated as no name: the section's tasks join the one before, with the existing warning, and the title line is left out.
triage.cause: `!== undefined` used where an empty-text test is needed

claim: The gantt and journey readers drop the accessible title silently when a title statement names the chart
Block reader: a group id given twice, or shared with a block, gives two items with one id
Class and ER writers drop a connector's dash pattern without a warning

triage.scenario: an edge with `colors.dash = [2, 6]`. All three writers write any dash as a dotted line (`..`, `..`, `-.-`), and each reader reads that back as `[4, 4]`. The class and ER writers list `dash` as kept in `dropEdgeColors`, so nothing warns. The block writer warns about stroke, label and width, but not dash. The pattern changes with no warning. The flowchart writer handles the same case properly, writing the custom pattern as a `linkStyle … stroke-dasharray`, so the kinds answer one question two ways. Expected: a warning whenever the dash is not `[4, 4]` (or not `DOTTED_DASH`).
triage.cause: "has a dash" is checked, not which dash

claim: Class writer loses the solid/dashed distinction of open vs filled arrows without a warning
Class writer silently drops namespace and note colors, and notes' namespace membership
Class writer keeps extra name lines as members in one case and silently drops them in the other

triage.scenario: rows `[label A, label B, divider, label x, divider, label m()]` give `names = [A, B]`. With two dividers (`rest.length > 1`), attributes are `rest[0]` and `B` vanishes without a warning. With zero or one divider, `names.slice(1)` is kept as members. The same second line is kept on one path and dropped on the other.
triage.cause: names.slice(1) left out of the divided branch

claim: C4 relationship technology given with an empty label comes back as the label after a round-trip

triage.scenario: `Rel(a, b, "", "HTTPS")`. The reader builds the label from `[text(label), "[tech]"]` and gets `[HTTPS]`. On write, `/^(.*?)(?: \[([^\]]*)\])?$/` needs a space before `[`, so `m[1]` is `[HTTPS]` and `m[2]` is undefined. The output is `Rel(a, b, "[HTTPS]")`, which moves the technology into the description/label argument. The element path (`elementParts`) keeps the two apart, but the relationship path does not. The writer regex should also take a label that is only `[tech]`.
triage.cause: label/technology split regex requires a leading space

claim: Block writer wrongly warns that a grid skip of 0 was dropped

triage.scenario: a grid layout whose `skips` gives an item `0` (no gap). `gridCount` rounds it to 0, finds `whole < 1`, and warns "Mermaid block spaces are whole numbers from 1; others were dropped." The output is right (no `space` line), but the warning reports a loss that did not happen. A skip of 0 should be read as no skip, with no warning.
triage.cause: gridCount's lower bound of 1 is applied to skips, where 0 is valid

claim: The flowchart lexer skips the newlines inside `@{ … }` metadata without counting them, so every later line number is wrong
Block writer moves a group holding no blocks to the end of its row, shifting the grid on round-trip

triage.scenario:
`block-beta
 columns 3
 a
 block:g
 end
 b` reads into nodes a, b and an empty container g. On write, `first({cluster: g})` is `Infinity` (no nodes), so `level` sorts g after b and emits `a`, `b`, `block:g end`. g moves from grid cell 2 to cell 3, and b from 3 to 2. The reader kept g's position in its parent's `members` order, which the writer ignores. Top level has no members list at all, so the order is guessed from node order.
triage.cause: item order derived from first node index; empty clusters have none

claim: Lexer reads A--oB / A--xB as an open line to node oB instead of a circle/cross edge to B

triage.scenario: the tail `[ox](?![\p{L}\p{N}_])` refuses a head that is followed by a letter. `A--oB` therefore lexes as link `--` (no head, and not opening a label, because the next char is not whitespace) followed by the word `oB`. The result is edge A→oB with `markerEnd: null`. Mermaid's lexer (`\-\-+[-xo>]`) takes `--o` greedily, which gives A→B with a circle end. Mermaid's own docs warn about exactly this reading for ids that start with o/x. The import silently produces a different graph (a node `oB` instead of `B`, and the wrong end).
triage.cause: lookahead diverges from Mermaid's link token

claim: The gantt writer writes `after <id>` for an id it just dropped, leaving the next task pointing at a task that doesn't exist
The class writer writes a `note` shape's text from `lines` only, so a note whose text is in `rows` is written empty
Architecture writer lets a service id be `accTitle`/`accDescr`, so its edges read back as accessibility text
Flowchart lexer splits A--text-->B (link text with no space after --) into three nodes instead of one labeled link

triage.scenario: `opens` is true only when the `--`/`==`/`-.` is followed by whitespace. For `A--text-->B`, the lexer emits `--` as a link with no end, then the word `text`, then `-->`. The parser builds the chain A --- text --> B: a phantom node `text` and two edges. Mermaid's START_LINK rule (`\s*[xo<]?\-\-\s*`) allows no whitespace there, so Mermaid reads one edge A→B labeled "text".
triage.cause: link text opens only when whitespace follows

claim: Flowchart writer writes an explicit solid dash (`dash: []`) as a dotted/dashed Mermaid line

triage.scenario: a graph page whose edge has `colors: { dash: [] }` (solid, as `paint.ts` and the DOT and draw-XML writers read an empty dash; Mermaid's own `dashOf` also yields `[]` for `stroke-dasharray:` with no value) is written with `dash !== undefined` as the test, so the flowchart writes `-.-`/`-.->`, the block diagram `-.-`, the class diagram `..`, and the ER diagram `..`. Read back, those edges carry `dash: [4, 4]`, so a solid connector turns dotted. It should be written as a solid line, the way the DOT writer's `dash.length > 0` test treats it.
triage.cause: the Mermaid writers and the other writers decide "dashed" differently (`!== undefined` against `length > 0`)

claim: Front matter `config:` is dropped silently, though the same settings in a `%%{init}%%` directive are reported
The architecture writer replaces a connector port that isn't a compass side with R/L, with no warning
Block writer silently drops or clamps link widths other than 3
Block writer turns any dash pattern into Mermaid's dotted link without a warning

triage.scenario: an edge with `colors.dash: [10, 2]` is written as `-.-`, which reads back as `[4, 4]`. The function warns about stroke, label and width but never about dash, whereas the flowchart writer keeps a non-dotted dash through `linkStyle` and other kinds call `dropEdgeColors`. The pattern changes silently.
triage.cause: dash missing from dropped-style warnings

claim: gitGraph writer spells a main branch name containing " differently in front matter and in branch statements, so the file fails to read back

triage.scenario: `mainBranch: 'a"b'`: the front matter writes `mainBranchName: "a\"b"` (JSON, which keeps the quote). Every command naming that branch goes through `branchName` → `quoted`, which turns `"` into `'`, giving `checkout "a'b"` / `merge "a'b"`. On read the main branch is `a"b`, and `checkout a'b` names a branch never made, so `replayGitGraph` errors and `readMermaidGitGraph` throws.
triage.cause: one name encoded two ways in one file

claim: Gantt writer leaves ';' unescaped in names, titles and sections, and '#'/';' raw in task ids, so Mermaid's gantt lexer cuts the token short

triage.scenario: a gantt task named `Build; test`, or a section or title holding `;`, is written as-is (spelledLine spells only `#` and `:`). A task id `a#1` or `a;b` passes `plain` (it checks only whitespace, commas and tag words) and is written raw after the colon. Mermaid's gantt grammar reads task data as `":"[^#\n;]+` and titles and sections up to `#`/`;`, so real Mermaid truncates or rejects these lines. The package's own reader doesn't treat `;` as syntax, so a round-trip test passes while the file breaks in Mermaid. The journey writer handles the same characters (it strips `#` and `;`), so the two kinds disagree.
triage.cause: spelled set missing `;`; id check missing `#` and `;`

claim: Block parser reads a line with two link operators in a row followed by two blocks as a chain instead of rejecting it

triage.scenario: `a --> --> b c` (or `a b --> --> c`) collects items `[a, b, c]` and two links. The check only compares counts (`ends.length === links.length + 1` and `ends.length === items.length`), not that blocks and links alternate, so it passes and reads as `a → b → c` instead of throwing "cannot read … as blocks joined by links". The order in which items and links appeared is never recorded.
triage.cause: count check instead of alternation check

claim: Block reader treats a pending `space` two ways depending on the statement
The flowchart and block readers read lean-left and inverted-trapezoid shapes as their mirror images, without a warning
mermaidIds treats flowchart keywords case-insensitively, so End, Graph and Style nodes are needlessly renamed

triage.scenario: `words` lowercases every keyword, and `valid` tests `words.has(id.toLowerCase())`. A node whose id is `End` or `END` (Mermaid's own documented fix for the `end` trap) or `Style` is judged reserved and written as `End_`. The flowchart reader's keyword checks are case-sensitive (`word(t, 'end')` in parse.ts, and `REST_KEYWORDS.has(word[0])` in lex.ts), so `End` would read back unchanged. Result: a flowchart with `Start --> End` comes back as `Start --> End_`, with the node's id changed.
triage.cause: case-folded keyword set vs case-sensitive reader

claim: A gitGraph directive that sets only the main branch is still warned as dropped when the branch name holds an apostrophe

triage.scenario: `%%{init: {"gitGraph": {"mainBranchName": "O'Brien"}}}%%`. `BRANCH_NAME` reads the name correctly. `directiveJson` then replaces every `'` with `"`, the JSON fails to parse, and `onlyMainBranch(null)` is false. `directives` is not decremented, so `readPageName` warns that the configuration directives were dropped, although the only thing they set was read.
triage.cause: blanket quote replacement corrupts values that contain apostrophes

claim: `metaEnd` treats an apostrophe inside a plain metadata value as an opening quote, so `@{ label: it's done }` throws "never closed"
Flowchart node metadata keys other than shape and label are dropped without a warning

triage.scenario: `A@{ shape: rect, icon: "fa:user", w: 80, img: "x.png" }` reads only `shape` and `label`. `icon`, `img`, `w`, `h`, `pos`, `constraint` and so on vanish, and the import's warnings never mention them. Every other unsupported input in these readers is reported through `warnings.list(...)`.
triage.cause: option silently dropped on one path

claim: Class and ER writers rename ids their own readers accept (hyphens, namespace dots)
Block reader: a `space` before a links line lands on a later block, not the link line's first new block
Architecture writer drops an empty service title, and the reader then labels the service with its id
Block reader accepts `columns 0` and `block:id:0` without a warning, and the writer then drops them

triage.scenario: `block-beta\n columns 0\n a b`. The parser reads n=0 and `walk` sets `top = 0`, which the grid layout then clamps to 1 with no warning. Writing that page back, `gridCount` drops the 0 and warns "whole numbers from 1". So the reader and writer disagree about whether 0 is a valid count, and the read gives no warning for a value the page does not honor.
triage.cause: no validation of counts on read

claim: Journey writer checks a title or section name for emptiness before stripping its syntax characters, so a name that is empty after stripping is still written

triage.scenario: `data.title` is `"#;"` or a section is named `":"`. The guard (`data.title?.trim()`, `section.name.trim() !== ''`) tests the raw text, then `plain` strips every character, so the writer emits a bare `  title ` or `  section ` line. Mermaid's journey grammar needs text after `title`/`section`, so the file fails to parse there. The local reader accepts it, which hides the problem. Step names avoid this because `stepName` runs after `plain` and falls back to `(untitled)`. The emptiness test should run on the stripped text, as it does for steps and actors.
triage.cause: emptiness checked before `plain`, not after

claim: Flowchart reader loses the `v` direction: it upper-cases the header's direction, then looks up the lowercase key
C4 reader accepts BiRel_U, BiRel_Back and RelIndex_Back, which the writer cannot produce, and reads BiRel_Back as one-way

triage.scenario: `REL` allows any of `Rel|BiRel|RelIndex` with any suffix. `BiRel_U(a, b)` reads with ports n/s, but the writer says "Mermaid C4 has no direction for a two-way or backward relationship" and drops them. So the reader and writer answer differently whether a two-way relationship has a direction. `BiRel_Back(a, b)` takes `back` and sets `markerEnd: null`, so a relationship named bidirectional reads as a one-headed backward arrow.
triage.cause: reader grammar wider than the macros Mermaid and the writer have

claim: Flowchart reader drops every plain mention of a node whose id is also some link's id

triage.scenario: `flowchart TD\n  A e1@--> B\n  e1 --> C`. `edgeIdsOf` collects `e1`, and `mention` returns early for any ref `e1` that has no shape. It does that whether or not the ref carries `@{…}` metadata. So node `e1` is never created, and a spurious "edge metadata was dropped" warning is raised. `link()` still pushes an edge `e1 → C` to a node that does not exist. The early return should apply only to a ref that carries metadata (`ref.meta !== undefined`) and is not otherwise a node.
triage.cause: edge-id test ignores whether the ref has metadata

claim: The gantt writer writes task ids raw, so an id holding a comma or starting with a tag word's syntax breaks the line
Architecture and C4 writers drop the page direction without a warning

triage.scenario: a graph page with `direction: 'down'` (or `'up'`/`'left'`) and notation `architecture` is written. Mermaid architecture has no direction statement, and `readArchitecture` always reads `direction: 'right'`, so the round trip turns the page sideways and `warnings` says nothing about it. `writeC4` likewise never reads `page.direction`. Every other dropped property in these writers (positions, styles, labels, ports) gets a warning.
triage.cause: missing drop warning

claim: A block group whose id looks like `block-N` is written anonymous, so edges and styles naming it read back as a new block
Mermaid detect accepts any-case flowchart headers that the reader then rejects
C4 writer turns a deployment node whose type is "system", "container" or "enterprise" into a boundary macro
Class relation to a class whose id starts with `o` reads as an aggregation to a truncated id
Class diagram reader throws on nested generics

Block parser accepts a dangling trailing link operator (`A B -->`) and creates an A → B edge instead of a syntax error

C4 `<<person_db>>`/`<<person_queue>>` rows are accepted as a kind but written as a macro the reader refuses, so the element is lost

triage.scenario: the reader yields name row `<<x>>` for `class A["<<x>>"]`, or a user names a box `<<Service>>` with no annotations. classParts treats every `<<…>>` line above the first divider as an annotation, so the class is written as `class A { <<x>> }`. The label is gone and an annotation has been added. The writer never spells the brackets to stop this.

claim: GitGraph export rewrites " to ' in branch names, so distinct branches collide and reimport rejects a duplicate branch

`headerWord` treats an unclosed `---` as front matter running to the end, so detect says no

Class and ER writers silently drop a box's header rows, losing the class/entity name
